title: Proslogium, Monologium and Cur Deus Homo
author: anselm
attributionNote: Anselm wrote these treatises as abbot of Bec and archbishop of Canterbury. The appendix prints Gaunilo of Marmoutiers' reply on behalf of the fool and Anselm's answer to it, both of which circulated with the Proslogium from the beginning.
description: Anselm's three treatises are the beginning of scholastic theology. The Monologium argues from the existence of good things to a single highest good; the Proslogium seeks one argument that needs nothing beyond itself, the famous proof that God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, and ends in the prayer that God may be known and loved; Cur Deus Homo asks why God became man and answers with the theory of satisfaction that shaped Western soteriology. With them the volume prints Gaunilo's objection and Anselm's reply, the first philosophical critique of the ontological argument.
historicalContext: Anselm wrote the Monologium and Proslogium at Bec in the 1070s and Cur Deus Homo in England at the end of the century. Sidney Norton Deane's translation, published by the Open Court Publishing Company in 1903, made the treatises available to English readers with the objections of Gaunilo and the later philosophers on the ontological argument.
availabilityNote: Complete. The Proslogium, the Monologium, the appendix with Gaunilo and Anselm's reply, and both books of Cur Deus Homo are streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one chapter per chapter. The archive prints each book of Cur Deus Homo as a single page, so the two books are two long chapters; the rest of the volume (introduction, bibliography, indexes) is not part of the work.
